tagline.text: A 27 m waterfall in Pagudpud, reached through bamboo groves and streams

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May (avoid the rainy season and the days right after typhoons)

children.text: From Barangay Balaoi in Pagudpud, a walk of about 30 minutes along rice-field dikes and across small streams leads to a waterfall about 27 m high and a clear, cold pool. It combines easily with Saud Beach and the Patapat Viaduct in a half-day trip.
Kabigan Falls is hidden in the forest behind Barangay Balaoi in Pagudpud, Ilocos Norte, near the northwestern tip of Luzon. The drop is reported to be about

(87 ft), and the water lands in a bowl-shaped pool at the base. Mossy rocks and old trees surround the falls, which gives the place the feel of a secret spot deep in the woods. Even at midday the shade keeps it cool, and the water is cold enough to refresh you after a sweaty walk.
The falls are popular because they are easy to reach. Sources give the walking distance from the highway as
, and the walk takes about
20–30 minutes

one way. The path passes rice-field dikes, a bamboo grove, small streams and a wooden bridge, so it feels more like a country walk than a mountain hike. You do have to cross streams and step on wet rocks, though, so bring shoes that can get wet.

The origin of the name is unclear, but one explanation says it comes from the Filipino word kaibigan, meaning friend. The Pagudpud municipal government manages admission and guiding, and the usual routine is to register at the entrance and go in with a local guide. A guide does more than show the way: he or she also knows which rocks are slippery and how far you can go in the water when the stream is high, so the fee is money well spent. How long does it take? One traveler reported arriving at 1:00 pm, walking in with a guide, and being back at the highway around 2:30 pm. If you only take photos and rest a little, allow about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
for the round trip. If you swim for a long time or have lunch, it becomes a half-day outing. Some accounts also describe the roughly

stretch from the highway into the village as a paved access road, which may explain why the walking distance differs from source to source. Ask your guide at the entrance how far today's route actually is.

Kabigan Falls is most useful as one stop on a tour of northern Pagudpud. Bantay Abot Cave, the Patapat Viaduct and the Blue Lagoon lie along the same road, and you can reach the falls by tricycle from a Saud Beach resort. If you spend a day on the beach, giving one morning or afternoon to the falls is an easy plan. This page covers the waterfall itself in depth; for the beaches and the town as a whole, see
Pagudpud

blocks.title: A hidden waterfall about 27 m high

children.text: The water drops from a crevice in the rock into a bowl-shaped pool. Because the falls are tucked inside the forest, you hear the water before you see it as you round a bend. Plenty of trees keep it cool even at midday.

blocks.title: A path through rice-field dikes and bamboo

children.text: Leaving the highway for the village, you pass rice fields, a bamboo grove and small streams. You get a close look at rural northern Ilocos, and many travelers say the walk is as memorable as the falls.

The pool below the falls is wide enough to swim in. The cold water is a shock at first, but it feels great after walking on a hot day. The depth is uneven, so swim only in the area your guide points out.
Moss covers the rocks around the falls and large trees ring the pool, so photos come out green. Early in the morning there are fewer people and the light is soft.

blocks.title: A village path with a local guide

children.text: You register at the entrance and walk with a village guide. Besides directions and safety tips you may hear stories about the village, and the guide fee goes to local income.

blocks.title: A good fit for a northern Pagudpud tour

children.text: The falls lie in the same direction as Saud Beach, the Blue Lagoon, Bantay Abot Cave and the Patapat Viaduct. They are a common stop on the northern tricycle tour, and a half day is enough if you come only for the falls.

blocks.title: Easy enough for families and beginners

children.text: The round trip is short and the climb is gentle, so children of elementary-school age and older can usually manage it. Adults should still hold a child's hand over slippery rocks and stream crossings.

items.title: Half-day course
items.subtitle: Morning at the falls, then a loop around the north

children.text: Have a light breakfast at your Saud Beach lodging and arrange a tricycle. Agree before leaving on the fare to the falls and whether waiting time is included.

Walk back the same way and change out of wet clothes. Have lunch with Ilocano food at a restaurant near the highway.
Stop at Bantay Abot Cave and a viewpoint on the Patapat Viaduct before returning to your lodging.
Guide fees and admission differ between sources, so check the posted fee list first when you arrive.

items.title: Full-day northern course
items.subtitle: From the falls to the Blue Lagoon

children.text: Arrange a northern tricycle tour in town or at Saud Beach. A common route is Kabigan Falls, Bantay Abot Cave, the Patapat Viaduct and the Blue Lagoon.
Put Kabigan Falls first. Mornings have fewer people and avoid the midday heat.
Return from the falls and stop at Bantay Abot Cave to look at the sea through the hole in the hill.
Have lunch at a restaurant on the Blue Lagoon side. Light dishes such as grilled fish and sinigang are a safe choice.
Stop at the Patapat Viaduct and walk along the road between the cliffs and the sea.
Return to Saud Beach and watch the sunset.
Tour fares are bargained per tricycle (up to three passengers). Falls admission and the guide fee are usually separate.

15–20 minutes

items.title: Getting around from town and the beaches

children.text: From Pagudpud town to the Balaoi village entrance it is about
15–20 minutes
by tricycle.
The northern tricycle tour (Kabigan Falls, Bantay Abot, Patapat and the Blue Lagoon) costs about
per tricycle (2026 guide; varies with bargaining and waiting time), which seats up to three people.
Because this is on the road that Manila-bound buses use, you can also flag down a bus on the highway when you continue to your next destination after the falls.
The dry season from
November–May
is best for walking. The streams are shallow and easy to cross, and the rocks are less slippery. Note that the northeast monsoon makes the coast rough from
November–February
, and daytime temperatures are high from
March–May
, so go in the morning.
In the rainy season from
June–October
the falls swell and look more powerful, but heavy rain can close access and make the streams hard to cross. Typhoons often pass Pagudpud from
July–September
. If you go then, check the PAGASA forecast and local announcements, and leave one spare day in your schedule.

rows: Cool and relatively dry, northeast monsoon
Streams are shallow and walking is easy, but waves can be high on the coast
Best for swimming, go in the morning, Holy Week and May holidays are crowded

Most people stay at Saud Beach or the Blue Lagoon and visit the falls as a day trip. Resorts at Saud Beach cost about
a night, and rooms in town and roadside guesthouses are around
. They fill early during Holy Week and the May and December holidays, so book two to three weeks ahead.

The food is mainly Ilocano. Restaurants near the highway are said to serve typical Ilocano dishes such as dinakdakan (a pork specialty), dinardaraan (a blood stew) and pinakbet (vegetables cooked with shrimp paste). For seafood, grilled fish and kilawin, fish cured in vinegar, are common. There are few shops on the way to the falls, so bring water and snacks. ATMs are scarce in Pagudpud, so carry enough cash.
One record says there is a restaurant serving Ilocano food about
10 minutes

by car from the highway. Ask your guide or tricycle driver which place is open today, as that is the surest way to find out. Fresh coconut juice is easy to find at stalls on the beach side, which is a good way to quench your thirst after the falls.
Wear water shoes or trekking sandals that can get wet. Bare feet or slippery flip-flops are dangerous on the streams and rocks.
Wear your swimsuit underneath and carry dry clothes and a towel in a waterproof bag.
Going early means fewer people and less midday heat. Admission is listed as
, but confirm on site.
Fees differ by source. Check the fee list at the entrance and keep the receipt.
Bring small change. Guides and shops often take cash only.
Put your phone and camera in a dry bag. Water can splash or you can drop them while crossing a stream.
Carry your trash back out. There are few bins around the falls.
From a Saud Beach lodging, plan the falls in the morning and the beach in the afternoon to avoid the heat.
You return by the same path. If you plan to stay long at the falls, agree on a return time with your guide and arrive well before the last admission time.
After heavy rain the streams rise and become dangerous. Follow any closure, and leave right away if the water turns muddy or the sound suddenly grows louder.
The rocks below the falls are very slippery because of moss. Do not jump from high places.
During typhoon season (July–September) roads around Pagudpud can be closed. Check the forecast.
The forest has mosquitoes and insects. Bring long sleeves or repellent.
Phone signal is weak in places, so stay with your group.
There is no shop at the falls, so buy snacks and water at the entrance and keep your bag on dry ground such as a rock next to your guide.
It is about
15 minutes
by car beyond the falls entrance. It is a
